nodes.name: Publish webhook
nodes.notes: rawBody is required: the signature is computed over the exact bytes the app sent, and n8n's parsed JSON does not round-trip to the same string.

nodes.name: Verify signature
nodes.notes: Throws on a bad signature, an empty recipient list or a missing subject, so each shows up as a failed execution the app can see rather than a silent no-op reported back as success. Reads KOYA_PUBLISH_SECRET the same way 3/build/n8n/koya-proposal-delivery.json reads its webhook secret: $env first, $vars second, each one guarded, because a blocked $env throws rather than returning undefined.

nodes.name: Send via Gmail
nodes.notes:
THE NEWSLETTER GOES OUT FROM GMAIL, and that is the difference between a demo that sends and one that only says it did.

Resend refuses to deliver to arbitrary recipients without a VERIFIED DOMAIN. With its shared onboarding sender it will accept the API call, return an id, and deliver to nobody but the account owner. The queue would then record `sent` with a provider id against a newsletter that reached no subscriber, which is precisely the false success this system is built to refuse.

Gmail sends as the connected account, needs no domain and costs nothing. Its daily send cap is a few hundred recipients, which is the honest limit of this lane and is written on the admin page.

No onError override here on purpose: a failure has to reach the app as a non-2xx, so the queue row records the failure and retries rather than recording a send.

parameters.responseBody: ={{ JSON.stringify({ ok: true, providerId: $json.id || $json.messageId || $('Verify signature').item.json.idempotencyKey, recipients: $('Verify signature').item.json.recipients.length }) }}

nodes.name: Acknowledge
nodes.notes: Reached only after Gmail actually accepted the message, so a 200 here means a send happened. The app writes `sent` on this response and on nothing else.
